patients.summary: Healthy young delivery contractor who joined in 2022 and then had three trauma admissions: a 2025 bicycle crash with a right clavicle fracture, small pneumothorax and subclavian artery injury; a 2025 car crash with a left tension pneumothorax; and a 2026 crash with hemorrhagic shock, liver laceration and left femur fracture, managed without blood as a Jehovah's Witness.

documents.title: New Patient Call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Caller would like to establish here; moved his care because his old office stopped taking his marketplace plan. Works for himself doing deliveries, mostly mornings and evenings, so midday works best. No current health complaints, just wants a regular doctor. Booked new patient physical 9/13 at 1:20. Membership info and intake forms sent to his email. Asked him to have his old office send records; release form attached to the email.

documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
26M here to establish primary care. Previous PCP in the area, last seen there roughly two years ago for a sports-type physical. Feels well. No complaints today.

PMH: none. No hospitalizations. PSH: none.
Meds: none. No supplements.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
FHx: father with hypertension, diagnosed in his early 50s. Mother has hypothyroidism. No bleeding or clotting problems in the family that he knows of, no connective tissue disease.
SHx: self-employed delivery work, app-based, split between his car and a bicycle depending on the route and season. Lives alone in an apartment. Never smoked, no vaping. Drinks maybe once or twice a month. No drug use. Wears a helmet on the bike, seatbelt always.
Faith: Jehovah's Witness. He volunteered that he does not accept blood transfusion and asked that we know that. Noted in chart.

ROS: negative across systems.

Exam: well-appearing, fit. HEENT normal, TMs clear. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Skin without lesions of concern. Extremities with full range, pulses 2+ throughout. Neuro grossly intact.

PHQ-2: 0.

Assessment/plan:
1. Adult wellness, healthy 26 year old. Baseline CBC, CMP and lipids today. One-time HIV and hepatitis C screening, discussed and he agrees.
2. Tdap given; he cannot recall a tetanus booster since school.
3. Flu and COVID when the fall supply is in, nurse visit.
4. Road safety talk was short, he is already careful.
Records release signed for prior office. Recheck in about a year.

documents.title: Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Brandon, everything from Tuesday came back fine. Blood counts, kidney and liver tests, sugar and cholesterol are all where they should be, and the HIV and hepatitis C screens were negative. Nothing to do. Good to meet you.

documents.title: Records From Prior Primary Care Office
documents.author: outside primary care
documents.body:

No problems listed, no medications, no known drug allergies. Childhood immunization record attached: MMR x2, varicella x2, hepatitis B series, polio series complete. No tetanus booster in the records since adolescence. No labs beyond a normal CBC in 2018.

Reviewed by PCP; nothing new. Immunization history abstracted.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary - Trauma Surgery
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, trauma surgery service
Admitted 01/12/2025, discharged 01/15/2025

Reason for admission: 28 year old male cyclist who came off his bicycle and landed on his right side, hitting the right shoulder on the curb. Helmeted. No loss of consciousness. Complained of right shoulder pain and trouble catching his breath.

Arrival: hemodynamically stable. Point tenderness over the right clavicle, breath sounds reduced on the right. Portable chest film showed a right clavicle fracture and a small right pneumothorax, no rib fractures, no hemothorax.

Hospital course: Admitted to trauma for observation of the pneumothorax. Several hours after arrival he developed swelling and bruising above the right clavicle. CT angiogram of the chest showed a focal intimal injury of the right subclavian artery with a small hematoma, no extravasation, no occlusion, distal flow intact. Vascular surgery consulted: nonoperative management, hourly then q4h right arm pulse and neuro checks, all stable through the stay. Hematoma did not expand. Pneumothorax managed with supplemental oxygen, weaned off on hospital day 2; repeat film 01/14 showed resolution. Pain controlled with oral analgesics. Arm in sling. Patient is a Jehovah's Witness; no transfusion was needed.

Discharge diagnoses:
- Right clavicle fracture, closed, nonoperative
- Small right traumatic pneumothorax, resolved
- Right subclavian artery intimal injury with supraclavicular hematoma, nonoperative

Discharge medications: oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg, 1 tab q6h prn severe pain, #16, no refills. May use plain acetaminophen for milder pain, not to exceed 3 g/day total.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: orthopedics in 3 weeks with x-ray. Vascular surgery in 6 weeks with repeat CT angiogram. PCP within 1 week. Sling for comfort, no lifting with right arm, no cycling or driving until cleared. Return for increasing neck or shoulder swelling, arm numbness, coldness or color change, or worse shortness of breath.

documents.title: Post-Discharge Call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt after hospital discharge 1/15 (bike crash, R clavicle fx, small PTX, subclavian artery injury on CT). Says shoulder hurts but manageable, using the oxycodone mostly at night and Tylenol during the day. Breathing normal. Swelling above collarbone about the same or smaller, no arm numbness, hand warm, normal color. In sling. Has ortho and vascular appointments. Booked with PCP Tues 1/21. Reviewed return precautions.

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 6 days after a bicycle crash. Discharge summary reviewed: right clavicle fracture, small right pneumothorax that resolved on oxygen, and a minimal intimal injury of the right subclavian artery on CT angiogram with a small hematoma, managed without surgery.

He is sore but better each day. Pain 4/10. Takes 1 oxycodone-acetaminophen at bedtime, plain acetaminophen otherwise. No shortness of breath. Hand feels normal. Not working for now.

Exam: uncomfortable moving the right arm, in sling. Yellow-green bruising above the right clavicle, soft, no pulsatile mass, no bruit. Tender over midclavicle with step-off. Right radial and brachial pulses 2+, equal to left. Hand warm, cap refill brisk, sensation and grip intact. Lungs clear, equal breath sounds both sides.

A/P:
1. Right clavicle fracture: nonoperative, sling, ortho visit set.
2. Right pneumothorax: resolved, clear lungs. Removing from active list.
3. Right subclavian artery injury: exam reassuring today. Keep vascular appointment and repeat CTA. Reviewed warning signs.
4. Pain: taper off the oxycodone this week; acetaminophen scheduled is fine. Avoid ibuprofen until vascular sees him.
No driving or riding until ortho clears him.

documents.author: orthopedics

Outside orthopedic group, clinic visit 02/05/2025

Thank you for sharing the care of Mr. Hastings, 28, seen 3 weeks after a closed right midshaft clavicle fracture from a bicycle crash. Pain much improved, now mostly with reaching. Sling on most of the day.

Exam: mild tenderness at the fracture, skin intact, no tenting. Neurovascularly intact right arm.

reports.text: CT angiogram of the chest with IV contrast. Comparison 01/12/2025. The right subclavian artery is of normal caliber with a smooth wall; the previously seen intimal irregularity is no longer evident. No pseudoaneurysm, dissection flap or stenosis. The supraclavicular hematoma has resolved. Healing right clavicle fracture. Lungs clear, no pneumothorax.
reports.conclusion: Healed right subclavian artery injury; hematoma resolved; no pseudoaneurysm.

documents.title: Vascular Surgery Clinic Letter
documents.author: vascular surgery
documents.body:
Vascular surgery clinic, 02/26/2025

Re: Brandon Hastings, DOB 06/19/1996

I saw him for follow-up of the right subclavian artery intimal injury identified during his January trauma admission and treated without intervention. He has had no arm pain with use, no numbness, coolness or color change of the hand.

Exam: supraclavicular area flat, no mass, no bruit. Radial pulses 2+ and symmetric. Arm blood pressures symmetric.

Repeat CT angiogram today shows a normal-caliber artery with smooth wall and resolution of the hematoma, no pseudoaneurysm.

Impression: healed minimal right subclavian artery injury. No further vascular imaging or follow-up needed. He may return to full activity from our standpoint once orthopedics clears the clavicle.

Allergies: NKDA. Medications: none.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary - Critical Care
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
Regional hospital, medical-surgical ICU
Admission 10/12/2025, discharge 10/16/2025

History: 29 year old man brought in after a motor vehicle collision. Known prior right subclavian artery injury from a bicycle crash in January of this year. On arrival he was hypotensive and tachycardic in marked respiratory distress.

Findings: no breath sounds over the left chest with hyperresonance to percussion, distended neck veins, trachea shifted toward the right. Clinical diagnosis of left tension pneumothorax.

Course: needle decompression of the left chest at once with a rush of air, followed by rapid improvement in blood pressure and heart rate. Left tube thoracostomy placed in the trauma bay. Post-procedure film: left lung re-expanded. Admitted to the ICU for monitoring. When able, he told the team he is a Jehovah's Witness and does not consent to blood products; his counts were stable and none were needed. No air leak after the first day. Tube removed on hospital day 3, follow-up film without pneumothorax. Transferred out of the ICU day 3, discharged home day 4.

Discharge diagnosis: left tension pneumothorax after MVC, treated with decompression and chest tube, resolved.
History: right subclavian artery injury (January 2025).

Medications at discharge: acetaminophen 1000 mg every 6 hours as needed. NKDA.

Instructions: keep chest tube site covered 48 h. No flying for 2 weeks. No heavy lifting for 2 weeks. See PCP within a week with a chest x-ray. Return for shortness of breath or chest pain.

documents.title: Chest Tube Placement
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Procedure: left tube thoracostomy, 10/12/2025, trauma bay.
Indication: left tension pneumothorax, already needle decompressed at the left second intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Consent: emergent.
Technique: left lateral chest prepped and draped. Local anesthetic. Incision over the fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line, blunt dissection over the rib into the pleural space, finger sweep, tube directed apically and posteriorly, secured with suture and occlusive dressing. Connected to suction with immediate air return and fogging.
Complications: none. Minimal blood loss.
Post-procedure film: tube in good position, lung re-expanded.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary - Trauma Surgery
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, trauma and acute care surgery
Admitted 07/06/2026 via trauma bay, discharged 07/22/2026 (hospital day 17)

Presentation: 30 year old man brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle collision, unresponsive, with multiple injuries. BP 80/50, HR 130, RR 24. Pale and diaphoretic. Abdomen distended. Obvious deformity of the left thigh. Arrival labs: hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, hematocrit 18%, platelets 250,000/uL, INR 1.9, lactate 6.4 mmol/L. Prior trauma history: right clavicle fracture and subclavian artery injury (Jan 2025), left tension pneumothorax (Oct 2025).

Blood products: A friend who arrived with him told the team he is a Jehovah's Witness and has always refused transfusion. There was no advance directive and he could not participate in decisions. After discussion among the trauma attending, ethics on call and nursing leadership, the team honored the reported refusal and managed him without blood products. On waking he confirmed that he refuses all blood products.

Course:
- Hemorrhagic shock with coagulopathy: tranexamic acid on arrival, crystalloid limited, damage-control laparotomy within the hour. Hemoperitoneum from a moderate laceration of the right lobe of the liver, hemostasis by perihepatic packing; temporary abdominal closure. Returned to the OR on day 2 for removal of packs; no further bleeding; abdomen closed. INR 1.2 by day 3. Lactate cleared.
- Neuro: unresponsiveness attributed to shock; he woke as perfusion improved. CT head normal. Extubated day 3, neurologically intact.
- Left femoral shaft fracture: displaced transverse midshaft fracture; external fixator placed the first night; converted to intramedullary nail on day 4. Weight bearing as tolerated.
- Anemia: hemoglobin nadir 5.4 on day 2. Managed with IV iron sucrose, epoetin alfa, folic acid and minimized blood draws. Hemoglobin 7.3 on the day of discharge.
- VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin once hemostasis was secure.
- Worked with PT; walking with a walker on discharge.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Multiple traumatic injuries, motor vehicle collision
2. Traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy, resolved
3. Moderate liver laceration, damage-control laparotomy with packing, subsequent closure
4. Closed left femoral shaft fracture, intramedullary nail
5. Acute blood loss anemia, refuses transfusion
Other history carried on the hospital problem list: right subclavian vessel injury; tension pneumothorax.

Discharge medications:
- oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg, 1 tab q6h prn severe pain, #28
- enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily, complete 4 weeks
- ferrous sulfate 325 mg PO daily
- folic acid 1 mg PO daily
Allergies: NKDA. Blood products: refused (Jehovah's Witness).

Disposition: home with walker and home PT.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with CBC; orthopedics 3 weeks with x-ray; trauma clinic 3 weeks for incision check. No driving while taking opioids. No lifting over 10 lb.
Return for fever, wound drainage, abdominal pain, leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or fainting.

documents.title: Operative Report - Exploratory Laparotomy
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Date of operation: 07/06/2026
Preoperative diagnosis: hemorrhagic shock, distended abdomen after motor vehicle collision.
Postoperative diagnosis: hemoperitoneum from moderate laceration of the right lobe of the liver.
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, perihepatic packing, temporary abdominal closure.
Anesthesia: general.
Blood products: none; patient's reported religious refusal honored. Tranexamic acid given in the trauma bay.
Findings: large hemoperitoneum. Laceration of the right hepatic lobe with ongoing venous oozing, no major hepatic vein or caval injury. Spleen, bowel, mesentery, stomach, pancreas and both kidneys without injury. No retroperitoneal hematoma.
Description: midline incision. Blood evacuated. Four-quadrant packing, then systematic exploration. Hepatic bleeding controlled with manual compression and perihepatic packs above and below the liver. Remainder of the abdomen explored and normal. Negative-pressure temporary closure placed.
Disposition: to trauma ICU, intubated, for warming and correction of coagulopathy, with planned return to the OR.

Return to OR 07/08/2026: packs removed, no rebleeding from the liver, abdomen irrigated and fascia closed primarily, skin left partially open with wicks.

documents.title: Operative Report - Femur Fixation
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
Date of operation: 07/10/2026
Diagnosis: closed displaced transverse midshaft fracture of the left femur, in external fixation since 07/06/2026.
Procedure: removal of external fixator; antegrade reamed intramedullary nailing of the left femur with proximal and distal interlocking screws.
Blood products: none, per patient's wishes, confirmed with him before surgery. Cell-conserving technique.
Findings: pin sites clean. Fracture reduced closed with anatomic alignment. Nail length and rotation confirmed on fluoroscopy against the opposite side.
Complications: none.
Plan: weight bearing as tolerated, enoxaparin prophylaxis, PT.

documents.author: physical therapy

Home health agency, PT start of care 07/24/2026.
Dx: left femoral shaft fracture s/p IM nail 07/10/26; s/p laparotomy for liver laceration.
Home: second-floor apartment, 12 steps with a rail. Lives alone; friend staying short-term.
Findings: alert, oriented, follows instructions. Left hip and knee motion limited by pain, left quad weak, right leg normal. Transfers with supervision. Gait with front-wheeled walker, weight bearing as tolerated, household distances. Stairs one at a time with rail and supervision. Vitals stable during session.
Plan: 2x/week for 4 weeks: gait training, stairs, quad and hip strengthening, transfers, home safety. Goal: independent with cane for community distances.
Plan of care sent for physician signature.

orders.reason: acute blood loss anemia, no transfusion

documents.title: Transitional Care Video Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit; Brandon at his apartment, on the couch with his leg up. Consent for telehealth given.

Discharge summary reviewed in full. Admitted 7/6 to 7/22 after a severe car crash: hemorrhagic shock with coagulopathy, liver laceration managed with damage-control laparotomy and packing then closure, left femoral shaft fracture with ex-fix then IM nail. As a Jehovah's Witness he received no blood; his hemoglobin bottomed at 5.4 and was 7.3 at discharge on IV iron, epo and folate.

Today: tired, naps in the afternoon. Walks room to room with the walker, home PT twice a week. Pain 4/10, using oxycodone-acetaminophen twice a day, mostly before PT and at night. Eating okay, bowels moving. Belly incision looks clean on camera, no redness or drainage. Thigh incisions closed. No calf swelling or pain. No fever. Giving his own enoxaparin each evening.

PHQ-2 0.

Medication reconciliation done against discharge list: oxycodone-acetaminophen prn, enoxaparin 40 daily through about 8/19, ferrous sulfate 325 daily, folic acid 1 mg daily. No other meds. NKDA.

We talked about blood. He confirms he declines all blood products and wants that clearly in our chart. It is.

Assessment and plan:
1. Acute posthemorrhagic anemia, no transfusion by patient choice: symptomatic but stable. CBC this week at our lab (he has a ride Thursday). Continue iron and folic acid.
2. Hemorrhagic shock and coagulopathy: resolved in hospital.
3. Liver laceration after damage-control laparotomy: healing, trauma clinic visit set for mid-August.
4. Left femur fracture with IM nail: WBAT with walker, home PT, ortho in 2 weeks. Enoxaparin to finish 4 weeks.
5. Pain: taper oxycodone as tolerated, acetaminophen between doses, not over 3 g/day total including the combination tablets. No driving on opioids.
In person with me in early September once he can manage the trip. Call sooner for fainting, shortness of breath, leg swelling, fever.

documents.body: Sounds like you're on the right track. Use plain acetaminophen during the day, keep the remaining tablets for after PT or bedtime, and let them run out. If the pain at ortho on the 12th still needs more, they can decide on that. Stay under 3 grams of acetaminophen a day total.

documents.title: Orthopedics Clinic Letter
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
Orthopedic trauma clinic, 08/12/2026

Mr. Hastings is 5 weeks from a left femoral shaft fracture, external fixation then IM nail on 07/10. Using a walker at home, a cane for short distances. Pain modest.

Exam: incisions healed. Thigh soft. Knee motion improving. Calf soft, nontender. Distal pulses and sensation intact.

X-ray: hardware in good position, early callus.

Plan: weight bearing as tolerated, transition to cane as balance allows. Finish the enoxaparin at 4 weeks from discharge, then stop. Outpatient PT referral placed for gait and quad strength. Return in 6 weeks with x-ray. Not cleared for delivery work or cycling.

Medications per patient: ferrous sulfate, folic acid, enoxaparin, acetaminophen; oxycodone-acetaminophen occasionally. Allergies NKDA.

documents.title: Trauma Clinic Letter
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Trauma and acute care surgery clinic, 08/14/2026

Seen for follow-up after damage-control laparotomy for a liver laceration and perihepatic packing in July. Eating normally, no abdominal pain, no fever. Energy improving.

Exam: midline incision healed, no hernia, no tenderness. Abdomen soft.

Hemoglobin today 10.1 g/dL.

Plan: no lifting more than 10 lb for 6 weeks to protect the abdominal wall. Continue iron per PCP. No driving while using opioids. Follow up with us as needed; orthopedics following the femur.

The hospital problem list still carries his 2025 right subclavian vessel injury and tension pneumothorax.

documents.title: Work Question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Trauma clinic said the belly looks good and my blood was 10.1. Any chance I can do car deliveries soon? I'm off the oxycodone as of this weekend. Bills are piling up.

documents.title: RE: Work Question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That's a big jump from 8.8, nice. Driving depends on your left leg strength and on ortho clearing you, and lifting packages is limited to 10 lb by the trauma team until late September. Let's go over it together at your September visit, and bring any forms the apps need.
